items.t: Chapter 9 (al-bāb al-tāsiʿ): On the occult properties of the openings of the firmly established (muḥkamāt) suras of the Qurʾān and of the clear verses

Know — may God, exalted is He, grant success to me and to you — that among the occult properties of the letters of the alphabet that stand at the openings of the suras, and of the letters of the alphabet in their entirety, and of what attaches to them of their effects in the matters of operative deployment (taṣrīf), is what certain of the scholars — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them — said concerning His saying, exalted is He, Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād (Q 7:1): its meaning is "I am God, I decide." And al-Ḥasan said: the alif is the alif of pre-eternity (azal); the lām is the lām of post-eternity (abad); the mīm is "from Him unto Him"; and the ṣād is the joining of whoever joins himself to Him and the severance of whoever severs himself from Him. Yet in reality there is neither joining nor severance. These expressions run according to the [spiritual] states, and the mines of the Real are guarded from utterances and expressions. Every name among the names of God, exalted is He, brings you to a rank among the ranks; but His name Allāh, exalted is

He, brings you to all the ranks, for it is the name of the Essence qualified by the holy attributes, and all the names go back to it. And whoever is made privy to its meaning is made privy to the meanings of the hidden names, which are the individual letters (al-ḥurūf al-mufrada). So understand the indications, and do not halt at the expressions — you will be among those possessed of certainty. And the first of the hidden names is Huwa (He), a name composed of two letters; and it is the locus set for the divine indication (al-ishāra al-ulūhiyya), to which the hidden and the manifest names all return.

Fāʾida (a useful point). When God, exalted is He, created the letters, He appointed for them the ranks of the secret in Adam — peace be upon him — and did not lodge it in the angels. So the letters ran upon the tongue of Adam — peace be upon him — in the diverse modes of running and in the kinds of languages. And God, exalted is He, set the form of all the letters within the heart as a spiritual reality, and it is that which appears in the utterance of the soul and in corporeal script. So there are letters in the breast, letters upon the tongue, and letters in the bodily [members]. To that points His saying, exalted is He: Ṣād. By the Qurʾān, possessor of the Remembrance (Q 38:1); Qāf. By the majestic Qurʾān (Q 50:1); Nūn. By the Pen and what they set down in lines (Q 68:1). And the letters point to the verses of the Book, a reminder for those possessed of understanding. Every letter has three stations, according to the three vowels: the fatḥ (a), the ḍamm (u), and the khafḍ (i). And the letters of prolongation and softness (ḥurūf al-madd wa-l-līn) [derive] from them, after the likeness of the elements: each letter is the counterpart of an element. The worlds are three: of the visible kingdom (mulkī), of the Dominion (malakūtī), and of the Omnipotence (jabarūtī); and each one of the three is corporeal, psychic, and spiritual — so they are nine. The numbers are nine, the celestial spheres are nine, and the natures and the senses are nine. So the correspondence became manifest. Search out, then, the secrets of number and of the letters, and you will light through them upon sublime gnoses in [their] conjunctions and separations, according to what is required by the All-Mercifulness (raḥmāniyya) and the Compassionateness (raḥīmiyya) /fol. 50v./ of "In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Compassionate"; for it is from "In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Compassionate" that the cosmos takes its nourishment, and eats and drinks. So consider the suras of the Qurʾān: you will find them to arise from the multiplication of six by nineteen, the result being sixty and fifty-four. For the sixty added to the fifty is one hundred and ten, and with the four the total came to one hundred and fourteen, the number of the suras of the Qurʾān. And the six is the perfect number, corresponding to the number of the days in which God, exalted is He, created the heavens and the earth and what is between them. And these three are divided out into nineteen: the heavens are nine, together with the Throne and the Footstool; and the earth is ten, [with] the elements and what is composed of them — mineral, plant, animal, jinn, and angels. And the letters that are the openings of the suras are arranged in five ranks: single, twofold, threefold, fourfold, and fivefold. As for their sum, it is seventy-eight, which the number of fourteen letters comprises after the removal of what is repeated.

Faṣl. The letters are of two divisions: dotted and undotted. The dotted is of the visible kingdom (mulkī), and the undotted is of the Dominion (malakūtī). Then the mulkī is of two divisions: dotted with two and dotted with three. Those dotted with three are the shīn ()and the thāʾ (:)the shīn indicates the assemblage that is dispersed, and the thāʾ indicates the assemblage that is gathered. Those dotted with two are the tāʾ ()and the yāʾ (:)the yāʾ is a manifestation in the kingdom of His felicity (yumn), and the tāʾ appeared in the Dominion. Those dotted with one are the qāf ()and the nūn (): the qāf appeared in everything whose place of manifestation is from Him, as in al-Qādir (the Powerful) and al-qalam (the pen); and the nūn appeared in everything that makes manifest, and everything that makes manifest encompasses that which is made manifest by it — as the light of the sun, and instruments, and the nūn of the pen, and the ink of the book whereby the secret of its matter is made manifest. And the thāʾ likewise is a gathering by which the subsistence of everything comes about, for it is everything through which there is subsistence. And the shīn likewise is an announcement of evil, as it is in al-sharr (evil). And the shīn is the fruit of what lies between the two relations, for every growing offspring, as in al-tamr (dates) and al-turāb (earth). And the shīn is the manifestation of complete differentiation in outward beauty, and in all [of these]: al-shanaʾān (hatred) and al-shatāt (dispersion) and al-shabāb (youth) — which is a branch of madness — and al-ashghāl (preoccupations); or else it is doubled with what is congruent to it among the letters, as in al-ʿishq (passionate love), al-shaʿaf (ardent love), al-shighār (exchange-marriage), al-ghishāwa (the covering film), al-ghashm (oppressive wrongdoing), and the like of that. And the nūn — its meaning is a manifester that makes clear, as the light of sense-perception, the light of the sun, the light of knowledge, and the ink of books whereby their secrets are made manifest; and the water of the rain-cloud (al-muzn), which brings to light the foremost of creation — that the position of the nūn in His word might be preserved. The essences have enfolded it: their outward, their inward, and what lies between the two. And likewise it is distinguished in its form by three marks, as is the case with the name that gives notice of the thing it names, and with the journey that gives notice of the characters of men, and the like of that.

And al-Ḥasan — may God, exalted is He, have mercy upon him — said: In the Qurʾān is the knowledge of everything; and the knowledge of the Qurʾān is in the letters that stand at the openings of the suras; and the knowledge of the letters is in lām-alif; and the knowledge of lām-alif is in the alif; and the knowledge of the alif is in the point; and the knowledge of the point is in the primordial gnosis; and the knowledge of the primordial gnosis is in pre-eternity; and the knowledge of pre-eternity is in the [divine] volitions; and the knowledge of the volitions is in the unseen of the Ipseity (al-huwiyya); and the knowledge of the unseen of the Ipseity is in the like of whom there is nothing (Q 42:11).

And it is said concerning Yā-Sīn (Q 36:1) that it is a name among the names of God, exalted is He, like the rest of the letters of the alphabet that occur at the openings of the suras. And these are the luminous letters, fourteen letters, unrepeated, and they are these:(alif), (ḥāʾ), (rāʾ),(ṭāʾ),(kāf),(lām),(mīm), (nūn),(ṣād),(ʿayn), (qāf),(sīn),(hāʾ),(yāʾ). And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — that he used to say: The openings of the suras are taken from the names of God, exalted is He.

And Abū l-ʿĀliya said: There is not a letter among them but that it is the key to a name among the names /fol. 51r./ of God, exalted is He. So the alif is from Ilāh (God); the lām from Laṭīf (the Subtle); the mīm from Malik (the King); the ṣād from Ṣādiq (the Truthful); the rāʾ from Rabb (the Lord); the kāf from Kāfī (the Sufficient); the hāʾ from Hādī (the Guide); the yāʾ from ʿAlīm (the Knowing); the ʿayn from ʿĀlim (the Knower); the ṭāʾ from Ṭayyib (the Good); the sīn from Samīʿ (the All-Hearing); the ḥāʾ from Ḥamīd (the Praiseworthy); the qāf from Qadīr (the Powerful); and the nūn from Nūr (the Light). And this is their form, according as Abū l-ʿĀliya arranged them:

He made the middle letter a letter of indication — namely the hāʾ and the yāʾ — and he placed first the letters of Alif-Lām-Mīm, Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād, Alif-Lām-Rāʾ, Kāf-Hāʾ-Yāʾ-ʿAyn-Ṣād, and Ṭā-Sīn; and the ḥāʾ from Ḥā-Mīm; and the qāf from Qāf. By the majestic Qurʾān (Q 50:1); and the nūn from Nūn. By the Pen (Q 68:1).
And Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them both — said concerning the meaning of Alif-Lām-Mīm (Q 2:1): its meaning is

"I am God, I know"; and Alif-Lām-Rāʾ (Q 10:1): "I am God, I see." So the alif conveys "I" (anā); the lām conveys the name Allāh; the mīm conveys "I know" (aʿlam); and the rāʾ conveys "I see" (arā). And this is their order: Alif-Lām-Mīm (Q 2:1), Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād (Q 7:1), Alif-Lām-Rāʾ (Q 10:1), Alif-Lām-Mīm-Rāʾ (Q 13:1), Kāf-Hāʾ-Yāʾ-ʿAyn-Ṣād (Q 19:1), Ṭā-Hā (Q 20:1), Ṭā-Sīn (Q 27:1), Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm (Q 26:1), Yā-Sīn (Q 36:1), [Ṣād](Q 38:1), Ḥā-Mīm (Q 40:1), ʿAyn-Sīn-Qāf (Q 42:2), Qāf (Q 50:1), Nūn (Q 68:1). Then what was repeated among them fell away, and there remained fourteen letters, unrepeated; for their letters are established in these fourteen suras, and the fourteen luminous letters came forth from these fourteen suras — the ones whose mention has preceded — and it is to them that Abū l-ʿĀliya pointed. Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — said: The openings (fawātiḥ) of the suras — they are the Greatest Name of God.

Fāʾida. The names in their entirety are the number of the degrees of the Garden. From them knowledge was separated out, and to them it returns; and from them the existent things appeared. So the existent things are a sign pointing to the Most Beautiful Names. The names have coursed through them as the spirits course through bodies, and have taken within them the place that the Command holds in relation to creation. So there is no existent thing, minute or great, high or low, but that the names of God, exalted is He, encompass it, in entity and in meaning. And what the name of Divinity (al-ulūhiyya) requires is comprehensive of the meanings of all the [other] names; and the names in their entirety expound its meaning and give expression to it. So it is the greatest of the manifest names in this respect. The alif, then, is an upright letter: from it the letters arose, from it they draw their supply, and it is their matter; so it is the counterpart of the Intellect, the Pen, the Throne, and the Tablet. Next after it comes the lām, which is the letter that joins the highest to the lowest, and its counterpart is the Tablet, the Footstool, and the Soul. And next after the lām comes the mīm, which is the letter that indicates completion, and its counterpart is the body. For the Intellect is the first created thing, and the body is the terminus of created things. And all the [other] meanings of the letters are contained within the alif; and in the alif is the meaning of gathering and of summary comprehension, just as the letters are summarily comprehended in the Pen. So understand the meaning of summary comprehension and of mutual interpenetration, and there will gleam forth for you precious spiritual secrets, the sciences of which reach [only] to inward finding (wijdān). So understand. Faṣl. Know that the friends of God (awliyāʾ) — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them — spoke concerning the science of the letters and of the names out of radiant lights that were made to flow upon them from the wellspring of [divine] election, upon the attainment of certainty in their hearts and of sincerity. So they were singled out, in the science of the names, above all others by three things. The first is that they were given to understand, of the meanings of the ninety-nine, by [divine] confirming support /fol. 51v./ and by inspiration, what others did not know by speculation and demonstration. The second is that they knew hidden names beyond these ninety-nine. The third is that they were singled out by being made privy to the Greatest Name of God. As for the prophets — peace be upon them — they knew of the meanings of the ninety-nine names, by the light of revelation, what the friends of God did not know by inspiration; and likewise they knew of the sciences of the hidden names and of the knowledge of the Greatest Name of God. And every name among these names — none knows it as it truly is save He who has named Himself by it and is qualified by its meaning, and that is God alone. And beyond all these names that God, exalted is He, has taught to His prophets and His friends —

— that behind which God, exalted is He, has veiled Himself in the world of the unseen: He has made none privy to it, neither a prophet sent [as messenger] nor an angel brought near. They said: The first thing with which God, exalted is He, singles out the servant, when He wills to take him under His patronage and to teach him the God-given science (al-ʿilm al-ladunnī) so that he becomes a knowing friend of God (walī), is that He should single him out, from the knowledge of the ninety-nine names, by [certain] special properties (khaṣāʾiṣ), so that there is opened to him from them, of knowledge, what is not opened to the [ordinary] scholar by the path of speculative reasoning. Then He raises him to the knowledge of the hidden names, the first of which is Huwa (He) — a name compounded of two letters, a locus for the divine indication to which the names, hidden and manifest, revert in their entirety, just as the manifest names reverted to the name Allāh, exalted is He. And after his knowledge of that, he learns the hidden names, which are the single letters, namely the fourteen letters that occur in the Qurʾān in the luminous openings of the suras, whose mention has already been made. And after he has understood them, God, exalted is He, bestows upon him the Greatest Name — that by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives. And the Greatest Name is taken only from al-Khaḍir — peace be upon him — according to the most widespread of the reports. Yet the friend of God may also receive it by inspiration, which is cast into his inmost being (rawʿ) when the breeze of mercy blows upon the servant. And the manner of its being received among the friends of God varies; the book would grow long with the exposition of it. And thereupon the earth is folded up for him, and he walks upon water, and he ascends through the air, and entities are transmuted for him, and other things besides among the charismatic marvels (karāmāt) with which the friends of God have been specially favoured. And all this is not a knowledge [drawn] from written pages; rather it is a special gift between a man and his Lord: whomever God, exalted is He, makes privy to it, He has taught it to him. And he — upon him be blessing and peace — said: ((All existence stands only by the names of God, exalted is He, the hidden and the manifest, the sanctified; and the alphabetic hidden names of God, exalted is He, are the root of everything among the affairs of this world and the next. They are the treasury of His secret and the concealed store of His knowledge; from them branched forth all the names of God, exalted is He; and they are those by which He decreed all affairs and which He deposited in the Mother of the Book.)) And Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — was asked about Kāf-Hāʾ-Yāʾ-ʿAyn-Ṣād (Q 19:1), and he said to the questioner: Were I to inform you of its interpretation, you would walk upon the water without your two feet being submerged.

And Sahl b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — said: /fol. 52r./ A man came to Ibrāhīm b. Adham and said to him: What do you say concerning Yā-Sīn (Q 36:1)? He said: Truly, in Yā-Sīnthere is a name — whoever knows it and calls upon God, exalted is He, by it is answered, be he righteous or dissolute; and when it is called upon for some matter, it is his own special possession. And it will come hereafter, if God, exalted is He, wills, in this book of ours.

Faṣl. And each letter of these fourteen letters that are in the openings of the suras has a meaning and a secret; when God, exalted is He, makes the servant privy to it, he attains a charismatic marvel from His own presence, or else he meets al-Khaḍir — peace be upon him. And it is soundly established in the hadith, from the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — that he said to his Companions: ((When you meet the enemy tomorrow, let your watchword be Ḥā-Mīm: they shall not be given victory.)) And Ḥā-Mīm (Q 40:1) is among the hidden, treasured names of God, exalted is He. Whoever attaches himself to its light, God, exalted is He, rends for him the customary order of things, and he attains benefits from its secrets. And Sahl b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — said: The noblest of all the letters are the nine letters; from their light the letters were clothed in beauty and splendour. And they are these: And the manifest bodies point to them and to their nobility, and they are the seven heavens, the Footstool, and the Throne; and these are the nine corporealized [realities] to which God, exalted is He, alluded in the Qurʾān in His words, exalted is He: Alif-Lām-Mīm (Q 2:1), Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād (Q 7:1), Alif-Lām-Rāʾ (Q 10:1), Qāf (Q 50:1), Nūn (Q 68:1), Ḥā-Mīm (Q 40:1), ʿAyn-Sīn-Qāf (Q 42:2), Kāf-Hāʾ-Yāʾ-ʿAyn-Ṣād (Q 19:1), Ṭā-Sīn (Q 27:1). And they are the fourteen letters. And it is said that they are the Greatest Name, the manifest and the hidden. And that which the masters among the people of realization, and the leading scholars among the people of the Law and of the Reality, have intimated is that the Greatest Name is Allāh among the manifest names, and consensus has all but been concluded upon it.

And the explanation of this Greatest Name is that it brings things forth from nonexistence into existence. The alif in it is an indication of the Noble Essence; and the hāʾ is a letter of encompassment, [fitted] for the reception of the secret, and it is the secret of the breast, since the breast is the secret of knowledge, in sum and in detail. And through it was the favour conferred upon the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace — in the words of the Real, exalted is He: Did We not expand your breast for you, and lift from you your burden?(Q 94:1–2). So the hāʾ is the secret of the expansion of the breast.

And since the alif is too exalted to be described by motion or by rest — on account of its separateness in the primordial things, and since to it belongs the terminus of all ends, so it is in the last [state]; for motion is bound up with the four aspects, ḍamm, naṣb, khafḍ, and sukūn, by way of a kind of determination, whereas it stands in no need of determination — it brought forth the first lām at rest, out of its own relation; then [the first lām] took on motion from the relation of what joined to it of the second lām, so as to receive the secret of its rest through motion. And the hāʾ receives it with a secret from the secret of the alif's rest, for as long as its powers endure; and the second lām receives that secret, and the second lām brings it forth, and it takes on motion from the relation of what joined to it of the second lām, by the secret of motion — for the second lām is its reality — and the second lām transmits it by the secret of its elevation. [Such is] its encompassment; and there are gathered in it the secret of motion and the secret of rest; and for this reason it was the hidden of the hidden, as God, exalted is He, said: He is God (Q 59:22), He is the Living (Q 40:65).

So the hāʾ is the secret of the expansion of the breast. /fol. 52v./ And the alif is the indication of the Essence; and the first lām is for the covenantal reference (al-ʿahd al-mīthāqī), by virtue of the secret of the alif's mediation contained in it. Then the second lām is for the reference of the cosmic regions (al-ʿahd al-quṭrī), by virtue of the secret of the alif contained in it. Then the second lām is for the compact of faith on the day of this world, for the acceptance of the obligation imposed by the Law, by virtue of the secret of the alif's mediation contained in it. Then the hāʾ is for the completion of the matter on the day of the last arising, for the gathering of the first and the last. So by this lordly wisdom there revolved a circle of fourteen letters, whose beginning is like its end and whose end is like its beginning, because the alif both precedes it and comes after it. The demonstration of that is that the alifs and the lāms are four; you multiply them by three, and it comes to twelve; and the hāʾ has a share of two; the total is fourteen, thus spread out. And they are these:— as he said, God bless him and grant him peace: ((He is the Manifest: there is none above Him; and He is the Hidden: there is none below Him.)) And since it is composed of fourteen letters, the seven heavens and the seven earths, and what is within them and what is between them of kingdom (mulk) and dominion (malakūt), subsist by a secret from among the secrets of the name of God, majestic is His remembrance. Thus in every atom of the atoms of the world, and in what is lesser than it, there is a secret from among the secrets of the name of God, exalted is He; and by that secret it understands from Him and bears witness to Him with [the confession of] the divine oneness. God, exalted is He, said to His prophet Muḥammad — God bless him and grant him peace: Do you know any namesake for Him?(Q 19:65). And He said, exalted is He: Say: "God!" Then leave them (Q 6:91).

And the imām, the gnostic of God, exalted is He, the erudite Fakhr al-Dīn al-Khwārizmī — may God, exalted is He, sanctify his spirit — said, in the sacred precinct of Mecca, in the year six hundred and seventy: Whoever knows God, exalted is He, by the name that exerts its efficacious influence upon his state and his station has come to know the

Greatest Name that is proper to him — just as He was Arḥam al-Rāḥimīn (the Most Merciful of the merciful) for Job — peace be upon him — when he said: Affliction has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful (Q 21:83); and when He was al-Wahhāb (the Bestower) for Solomon — peace be upon him — when he said: My Lord, forgive me, and bestow upon me a kingdom such as shall not befit anyone after me; truly You are the Bestower (Q 38:35); and just as He was Khayr al-Wārithīn (the Best of inheritors) for Zechariah — peace be upon him — when he said: My Lord, leave me not solitary, and You are the Best of inheritors (Q 21:89). So God, exalted is He, granted him John — peace be upon him — and granted Solomon a mighty kingdom, and restored Job to health from his affliction. So whoever knows the name that corresponds to his need and asks God, exalted is He, by it — He answers him and brings him to his desire.

And it was the practice of certain masters that, when a disciple came in upon him seeking the way of wayfaring (sulūk), he would seat him before himself and recite over him the ninety-nine names, while he looked upon his face as he uttered the names; and thereby the name suited to the disciple would become clear to the master, and he would command him to keep constantly to it, until through it a door of mercy would be opened to him from the name whose remembrance he had commanded him — for his name is the odd one (al-witr) within it, and by it the efficacious influence occurs in every person. And this is his aim.

And the knowledge of the Greatest Name of God is among the noblest of the sciences. The Greatest Name is a well-guarded pearl, kept safe from those who are not its people; it lies hidden among the most precious of treasures and stored up for the [secret] hoards. Over it have been pitched the pavilions of Might; before it has been let down the veil of Awe; around it has been extended the protected preserve of the Dominion (malakūt); and about it has been made to revolve the sacred precinct of the Omnipotence (jabarūt). So I set forth for it a similitude: the difficult questions of religion, which none attain /fol. 53r./ save the stalwarts among the divinely supported scholars. And among its grandeur, by which it is expounded, among the kinds of its nobility and its honour, is that those descriptions that are lofty and those noble epithets should be sent forth for it, and that there should be joined to it praiseworthy litanies of remembrance and glorious eulogies; and though their kinds differ, yet in declaring [God] transcendent and holy lies their gathering. And enough of good for you is the hearing of them, according to what the transmitted reports have brought concerning that, so that it may be the more magnificent in its remembrance, and greater for whoever hears it or recites it, and more precious to whoever repeats it and seeks it out. And it lies hidden within an ordering that is obscure or determinate. He has not summoned [us] to supplicate by it alone, nor have we been promised the answering [of prayer] by it alone, but rather together with noble names, attributes of ecstatic finding, mantles of eulogy and robes of praise. By it the compilations have been made resplendent, and by it the [scholarly] questions have been embroidered; the hadith of Anas has claimed the foremost place for itself, even though others share with it in the sources.

And among the wonders is that a supplicant should call and not be answered. And this Greatest Name is lacking in no act of worship, of whatever kind of the acts of worship it be, but that it is its root and its seal. It admits of neither dual nor plural, whereas all the [other] names admit of dual and plural; and that is a proof that all the names have drawn their light within the utterance of this Greatest Name — which indicates that it is the greatest of His names. God, exalted is He, said: To God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them (Q 7:180). So He annexed
— all the names to it, and arranged them in an ordered string in the remembrance that rests upon it. So this indicates that it is the greatest of them.

Another aspect. Know that all the remaining names are an attribute [predicated] of this Name, while it does not run as an attribute upon any one of them. So this indicates that it is the name of the Essence, and that what is other than it is the name of the Attributes; and the name of the Essence is greater than the names of the Attributes. This is plain and evident. And the proof of the soundness of this is that this Name is the emblem of faith, and [faith] is not complete without it, according to his words — upon him be blessing and peace: ((I have been commanded to fight people until they say: there is no god but God)); and nothing besides it suffices. So this indicates that it is the greatest of the names of God, exalted is He, and that it is what delivers from the Fire, according to his words — upon him be blessing and peace: ((Whoever dies bearing witness that there is no god but God, sincerely from his heart, God, exalted is He, makes him forbidden to the Fire)). And it is the key of the Garden, according to his words — upon him be blessing and peace: ((Whoever dies knowing that there is no god but God enters the Garden)). So this noble Name — by it one enters the Garden, and by it one is made forbidden to the Fire, and by it are faith and islām, and by it blood is spared, according to his words — upon him be blessing and peace: ((I have been commanded to fight people until they say: there is no god but God; and when they have said it, they have protected from me their blood and their property, save by its right, and their reckoning is with God, exalted is He)). And it is the key of the prayer, and the opener of the call to prayer and its seal; and no other suffices in its stead. And whatever has come down of the litanies of remembrance, the supplications, and the healing incantations (ruqā) — these are built upon the Greatest Name; for every supplication, however its kinds differ and the special properties of its names, is opened only with the Greatest Name — and that is Allāhumma ("O God"), in which the mīm has been added because it gathers all the names together by its encompassing. Then one finds among the obligatory works no work but that it falls within its compass — such as the prayer, which is the pillar of religion. The reason for this is that nothing suffices in the takbīr of consecration (takbīrat al-iḥrām), or in any other takbīr, except it; so /fol. 53v./ the prayer is not valid without it, by the agreement of the scholars of the great cities and of the righteous first generation among the forebears. And likewise the call to prayer: with it it is begun, and with it it is sealed.

Faṣl. This Greatest Name requires a name and a thing named; and this Name is among that whose knowledge God, exalted is He, has kept to Himself. I shall strike for you a similitude by which you may grasp what I apportion to you thereby. And that is: a man may know the name of a drug, and apprehend its meaning, its degree, its potencies, and its benefits; and after this apprehension he puts it to use. This is the rank of apprehending the expression, of verifying the meaning, and of employing it in what it requires. So when a man has apprehended the expression and verified its perfection, then this is the reality [of the matter]; there remains only the aspect of use, so that he comes to know the manner of its use and uses it therein. And there is no doubt that this is the reaping of the fruit and the completing of the benefit. And this is an aspect that admits of no distinction. The utterance has two states: one of them, that God, exalted is He, causes it to run upon his tongue without his knowing that it is the Greatest Name; and the other, that God, exalted is He, causes it to run upon his tongue and he knows that it is the Greatest Name of God. So does either of these two suffice, or does not one of them suffice, or does the second suffice without the first? In all of this there is room for consideration. And it may be said: by whatever means the disclosure of the Greatest Name of God, exalted is He, is obtained, God bestows the object sought. The least of that is its running upon his tongue, even if he is not aware that it is it. And this is the lowest of the degrees, and it is founded upon amplitude and upon the raising of expectation in the mercy of God, exalted is He. And that by which perfection accrues to the servant is his apprehending it in truth; and whatever falls short of that still contains blessing and good.

Disparity arises in that according to the levels of apprehension. And the proof of it: are they equal — one whom God, exalted is He, has singled out, so that He caused this Name to run upon his tongue, and one whom God does not single out with it and upon whose tongue He has not caused it to run — or are they not equal? It cannot rightly be said that they are equal; rather, he upon whose tongue it has run has a distinction indicating that its blessing has come to him, however that may be. And measure by this rank the ranks that come after it. And the apprehension of this Name is either by transmission, in that he is informed of it and it is said to him, "this is the Greatest Name" — and this is by way of acceptance on authority (taqlīd), whether from a prophet, or a saint, or an angel, or a dream, or something other than that. Or else his knowledge of it comes about by the practice of worship and by striving therein, until there is effused upon him a light from among the lights of God, exalted is He: this is the Greatest Name. Nor is it far-fetched that its attainment should come about by speculation and inquiry, together with the granting of success by God, exalted is He. And this Name was called "the Greatest" only for its indicating His particular ipseity; and it is said, for the multitude of its meanings and the universality of its encompassing, since it is the name that gathers and encompasses the names of God, exalted is He. And it is said: it was called "the Greatest" only because its apprehension depends upon true gnosis of it; so according to this saying its apprehension is not possible save for a prophet or a saint. And its apprehension may also depend upon a mighty condition — and to come to a stand upon the greatness is greater still than it. And it is said: it was called "greatest" only for the attainment of the mighty benefit for the one who supplicates by it, namely the answering [of the prayer]. And other things than this have been said, but we shall not lengthen the book by mentioning them. And the Greatest Name of God is greater than all of this, and more sublime.

And know that these seven letters that are absent from the Mother of the Qurʾān give notice of good — and this is the preponderant view — for the Thāʾ indicates firmness in affairs. God, exalted is He, said: its root is firm and its branch is in the sky (Q 14:24), the verse. And He also said — exalted be His praise: God makes firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the hereafter (Q 14:27). And He also said — mighty and exalted — to His prophet and His chosen one among His creation: And had We not made you firm (Q 17:74), and other such verses. As for the Jīm, it indicates bliss and the beautiful covering, because this letter stands foremost in the name al-jannāt (the gardens). God, exalted is He, said: Gardens of Eden, their gates flung open to them (Q 38:50). And the gardens, taken absolutely, are many and all-embracing. And it is one of the letters of jabr (restoration and compulsion), and for that reason it occurs in His name al-Jabbār (the Compeller), and al-Jalīl (the Majestic), and al-Jawād (the Munificent), and al-Majīd (the All-Glorious), and al-Mājid (the Glorious), and al-Jāmiʿ (the Gatherer). As for the Khāʾ, it indicates khayr (good). God, exalted is He, said: In them are good and comely women (Q 55:70). And He said, exalted is He: if he leaves goods behind (Q 2:180). And as for al-Khabīr (the All-Aware): He said, exalted is He: and God is aware of what you do (Q 3:153); and among His names — glorified and exalted is He — is al-Khabīr. As for the Zāy, it indicates zahw (bloom) and zīna (adornment). As for its indicating adornment, what it has of that comes from His words, exalted is He: And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps (Q 67:5). And He said, exalted is He: Made fair-seeming to men is the love of desired things (Q 3:14), the verse. And by zahw is meant the ripening of the fruits; and it is said: the adornment of the trees with fruit. As for the Shīn, it indicates al-shahīd (the witness) and al-shahāda (the bearing of witness), according to His words, exalted is He: God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those possessed of knowledge, upholding justice; there is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise (Q 3:18). And al-mushāhada (direct beholding) is ocular vision. And the martyrs (al-shuhadāʾ): alive with their Lord, provided for (Q 3:169). And drinking (al-shurb): He said, exalted is He: they drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor (Q 76:5). And healing (al-shifāʾ), according to His words, exalted is He: /fol. 54r./ And We send down of the Qurʾān that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers (Q 17:82). And he said — peace be upon him: ((The healing of my community is in three things: a verse from the Book of God, or a lick of the honey of bees, or a cup at the hand of a cupper — and in [another] transmission: or the scarification of a cupping-glass)). As for the Ẓāʾ, it indicates the outstretched shade and manifestation. God, exalted is He, said: and outstretched shade (Q 56:30). And He said, exalted is He: upon which they mount up (Q 43:33). And He said, exalted is He: and they became the uppermost (Q 61:14). So it indicates the winning of what is desired. And among His names, exalted is He, is al-Ẓāhir (the Manifest). As for the Fāʾ, it indicates al-fiṭra (the primordial nature), al-fākiha (fruit), and al-fuṭūr (fissures). He said, exalted is He: the primordial nature of God, upon which He originated mankind (Q 30:30). And He said, exalted is He: Originator of the heavens and the earth (Q 35:1). And He said, exalted is He: do you see any fissure?(Q 67:3). And He said, exalted is He: rejoicing — they and their spouses, in shades (Q 36:55–56). And He said, exalted is He: and fruit of what they choose (Q 56:20). These, then, are more weighty than those.

And the Thāʾ, the Zāy, and the Jīm are cold letters, and their nature is the nature of water and of the moon; and this is the nature of the outstretched shade and of the Garden of eternal abiding. And the Khāʾ and the Shīn are both cold and dry, of the nature of earth and the nature of the combatant. And the Ẓāʾ is hot and moist. And the Fāʾ is hot and dry, of the nature of fire, and it has among the shining planets the Red One (Mars) and the Sun. And they are gathered together in seven names: the first, al-Thābit (the Firm), who makes the servants firm; and al-Jabbār (the Compeller), and al-Khabīr (the All-Aware), and al-Zakī (the Pure), and al-Ẓāhir (the Manifest), and al-Fard (the Sole), and al-Shahīd (the Witness). And the Thāʾ has not appeared in any one of His names, exalted is He, save in His name al-Wārith (the Inheritor) and al-Bāʿith (the Raiser of the dead), in the last rank, by the secret of the world that brings to naught. And it points to gathering in His name al-Bāʿith, and points to annihilation in His name al-Wārith. And these two names have no wayfaring (sulūk). And there is nothing among the letters of the alphabet that is pointed with three [dots] save the Thāʾ and the Shīn, on account of the Shīn's encompassing of all that is other than it, and the Thāʾ's permeation of what is below it. And it has no occult property save in the world of the lower bodies; and it is to the earth as the pegs — I mean the mountains.

And the Fāʾ is a hot letter; it exercises operative deployment in whatever the letters of heat exercise it in. And it is in the fifth degree of heat, and its shape is to be reckoned with in the letter Yāʾ, and the table of its number is eighty by eighty. And I have not come to know of the names of God, exalted is He, any that subsists by the secret of the Fāʾ save His name al-Fāṭir (the Originator), and al-Fāʿil (the Agent), and al-Fāliq (the Cleaver). The Shīn is cold, and its number is a thousand, and its secret is the secret of the Sīn, and so too its operative deployment. And there is nothing among the letters of the alphabet that bears three marks — the last rank of the Throne — and three shapes, except it. The Shīn gathers within its own essence three ranks: the rank of the units, of the tens, and of the hundreds. And the

Shīn occurred in [the words] shahida Allāh (God bears witness), and there branched out from it, within the Throne, three testimonies: the testimony of the angels, the testimony of those possessed of knowledge, and the testimony of those other than those possessed of knowledge. And thus was it created, since the tawḥīd (the affirmation of God's oneness) that is highest is [that which comes] from the Real to us, while the tawḥīd that appeared through the traces is from us to God, exalted is He; and the whole of tawḥīd is gathered together — I mean the lights of tawḥīd. And it is for this that the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace — gave notice of it concerning one who remembers lā ilāha illā Allāh: ((It ascends to the Throne, and the Throne quivers at it, and it is said to it: Be still! And it says: /fol. 54v./ [Not] until the one who utters it be forgiven.)) And that is because God, exalted is He — sublime is His power and exalted is His wisdom — when He knew that He is neither pictured in the imaginations of the servants nor given modality in their intellects, set up for them a created thing like themselves, and placed it in the highest of stations and the noblest of created things, and ascribed it to Himself. He said, exalted is He: the Lord of the glorious Throne (Q 85:15). And it is like the chamberlain to the king whom no one can reach to behold; so it is that which conveys the needs of the petitioners and executes his decree among his subjects, and it indicates the existence of the King and His fixity and the might of His sovereignty. And that is what the Messenger of God — God bless him and grant him peace — gave notice of by his words: ((God, exalted is He, wrote a writ and set it above His Throne: My mercy has outstripped My wrath. () And he said — God bless him and grant him peace — concerning Saʿd b. Muʿādh al-Anṣārī: The Throne quivered at his death — this indicating God the Exalted's good pleasure with him. So this points to what appears of the ordinances of the Sole King upon His Throne, that it may be known that in the Throne there appear the traces of the power that comes from al-Qadīr (the All-Powerful). For this reason the Shīn was the last letter in [the word] al-ʿarsh (the Throne), and so it belongs to the tawḥīd of the multiple worlds. And since the ordering according to the divine determination was such that to every throne a footstool was assigned, the Shīn was the throne of the letters — and that on account of the greatness of its office and the loftiness of its rank. And there was not found among the letters anything that would complete its throne save the letter Alif, since it is the root of the tree of the letters, while the Shīn is that at which the letters reach their end and their ascent; and there can come after it no branch save from its own inward. And likewise, before the Alif there can be nothing save what is from it. And since the shape of the Shīn is like the shape of the Alif, the correspondence of the Shīn in respect of shape is shared between the two, because the Alif is spread out into three letters — thus: alif (( —and the Shīn is spread out into three letters — thus: shīn ) So its relation was like its relation. And though something other than the Shīn be composed of three letters, it does not thereby become a throne for the Shīn, because it does not reach the utmost limit of correspondence and of firm rootedness. And it is for this that it comes first in His words, exalted is He: God bears witness (Q 3:18) — an.)

indication of the firm rootedness of tawḥīd and of the non-existence [of any other] in the two abodes, the two worlds, and the two comings-into-being. And the Shīn is a footstool for the throne of the Alif, because every subtle thing is a throne and every dense thing a footstool. Nor is it far-fetched that the Footstool should be the bearer of the Throne, for you see that the whole body is a footstool for the throne of the soul. And in reality every subtle thing subsists by every dense thing. For this reason the Alif was the lightest of the letters and the subtlest, for the absence of any likeness to it and for its being set up as a diameter standing upright; and there is no likeness to it among the letter-units, nor is there any determination laid upon it from anything else; nothing else precedes it, and nothing else comes after it at the end of the word. So it, /fol. 55r./ together with the tens and the hundreds, points to firstness and lastness — except that the world of the Footstool is denser in relation to the world of the Throne. Do you not see that the Footstool is the locus of the forms, and the Throne the locus of the lights effused upon all the parts of the upper world? And the Alif has one aspect, [that of] the units and the thousands, while the Shīn has two aspects: an aspect in the hundreds — for when it is stripped of the dots it becomes a Sīn, and the Sīn is three hundred — and an aspect in the thousands. And that is because whoever contemplates the letter Shīn and knows its realities beholds the wonders of the things God, exalted is He, has made, and witnesses the secrets of the operative deployments of the letters.

And just as the Shīn was the last rank of the Throne in sum, so its last in detail is the Nūn, thus: shīn (.) And the Nūn is the bearer of the engendered beings — I mean the Whale that bears the world upon its back. And the Nūn draws its supply from the Shīn, and the engendered beings draw their supply from the Nūn. God, exalted is He, said: Nūn. By the Pen and what they set down in lines (Q 68:1). So the Pen draws its supply from the inward of the Nūn, which is the outward of the Command, which is the Kāf, whose inward points to the concealed secret; and that is the innermost secret of the Shīn. So whoever carries a written sheet upon which the letter Shīn has been written a thousand times, in the first hour of any day whose operation is suited to it — for among the days there are those in which good is sought and those in which evil is sought, such as Saturday and its hour, and Tuesday and its hour, and every day has what is suited to it for whoever knows it and understands it — whoever, then, knows this and puts it into practice, God, exalted is He, makes easy for him what he seeks and what he intends, of good or of evil.

And the secrets of the Shīn in the corporeal world are more than can be reckoned — save that one who has a pain in one of his limbs must not carry it, for he has no strength to withstand that pain, on account of a property within it — except the woman in childbed, for if she hangs the letter Shīn upon herself the delivery is made easy for her, with agitation. And it contains harm such as ought not to be disclosed. And this letter has occurred in His name, exalted is He, al-Shadīd (the Severe); so look there at what occult properties it contains. And whoever knows the rank of the Shīn, and where its relation to nature stands — in sum, and that is the Shīn of dryness, and in detail, and that is the Yāʾ and the Nūn — and what natures and numerical proportions belong to those two, has witnessed its secrets, and known its tidings, and known the receptivities and operative deployments that belong to it. And the ʿAyn draws its supply from the exaltedness above which there is nothing and beyond which there is no height; and the Rāʾ draws its supply from the mercy above which there is no mercy and below which there is no object of mercy; and the Shīn draws its supply from the witnessing above which there is no witnessing and below which there is no witnessed thing. So look how you find for witnessing a witnessed thing and a witnesser, and for mercy an object of mercy, yet you do not find for exaltedness any higher one nor any one exalting himself — because of the subduing of Lordship over servanthood, on condition of the necessity of obedience. To God belongs the might, and to His Messenger, and to the believers — but the hypocrites have no knowledge (Q 63:8). So the might that belongs to Divinity is the perpetuity of subsistence and pre-eternity; and the might that belongs to the prophets is the existence of the messengerhood; and the might that belongs to the believers is the existence of faith. And these are the three ranks of the Shīn in [the word] shahida.

Faṣl. And according to the first view, these seven letters give notice of torment; so you write them likewise for [inflicting] torment. You write the seven letters, beginning with the letter Shīn, then following the succession of the days and their letters, and you reverse the object sought; and you say in your invocation: /fol. 55v./ "...unless you take vengeance upon so-and-so son of so-and-so, and such and such." And you name whatever you wish of the kinds of torment, of affliction, and of vengeance — this after the writing of the letters according to its pattern, and after the day and the object sought are as they should be. And you say in your invocation: O Shadīd (Severe), O ʿAzīz (Mighty), O Wāḥid (One), O Ẓāhir (Manifest), O Wārith (Inheritor), O Jabbār (Compeller), O Fāṭir (Originator)! O God, O Shadīd, O Aḥad (Unique) after the passing away of His creation, by the command that You willed and the power that You determined! O You whose existence has no conjoining and no ending! O You whom nothing draws near save His own rank, and in whom there is no severance save by His rank! On a day when God will not put to shame the Prophet and those who have believed with him (Q 66:8). Surely the shame this day, and the evil, are upon those who disbelieve (Q 16:27). O You severe in torment and in punishment! Truly the seizing-grip of your Lord is severe (Q 85:12). As for those made wretched, they are in the Fire; theirs therein is braying and gasping (Q 11:106). Truly the tree of Zaqqūm is the food of the sinner; like molten dross it boils in the bellies, as scalding water boils (Q 44:43–46). O ʿAzīz, O Ghālib (Prevailer), O You who have no like and no peer, and with whom all needs lie! You are the absolute, beginningless Mighty One; none other than You bequeaths to You anything of Your might. O You who are manifest in power! O You who said — and He is the most truthful of speakers — By no means! It is Laẓā, the blaze, that strips away the scalp (Q 70:15–16), affording no shade, and of no avail against the blaze (Q 77:31)! O Wārith, You are the One to whom the whole affair returns, and existence too > and to You returns the whole affair <. O You who cause the engendered beings and those within them to pass away, and who call out: To whom belongs the kingdom this day? To God, the One, the All-Subduing (Q 40:16)! Everyone who has an invocation to make, in an outward or an inward matter, be it little or much, returns to You purely and under compulsion. O God, send down upon so-and-so woe and ruin and torment: Do not call this day for a single ruin, but call for many ruins (Q 25:14). O Jabbār, You are the One whose decree passes by way of compulsion upon every one; the wariness of the wary does not repel it. And You are the One who bound the powers of the soul and the powers of the heart within the densities of the bodies. That is incumbent only upon him who has been declared free of imperfection in what is due to You; and You made them a portion of Your ipseity, a manifestation of Your subduing-power, and an attribute of Your beginninglessness. So Yours are the strength, the omnipotence (jabarūt), the might, and the awe; and by the power of Your dominion (malakūt), which You chose by the eye of Your determining, and the judgements of Your divinity, and the lights of Your incinerating [powers] — none but You knows the meanings of Your affair and the greatness of Your sovereignty. For every motion in the world of the kingdom (mulk), of the dominion (malakūt), and of omnipotence (jabarūt) — a meaning among the meanings of Your names has lent aid by it, O Jabbār — by the right of what You have chosen, with the best of the beginningless, majestic, most exalted governance. O You who gave the world — that is, man — the choice by his motion, through what is within him of the secret of the life mingled with the spirit, by the reins of the measures and by [Your] leave — nay indeed! — until the world compelled one part of itself by the subduing of another, for the establishing of the subduing and the manifesting of wisdom: manifest in so-and-so son of so-and-so [woman] such of the severity of Your compelling and Your subduing as shall still his senses when he collides with me and quench his spiritual force when I am present! Truly Hell is the appointed place for them all (Q 15:43). And We have surely brought into being for Hell many of the jinn and of mankind (Q 7:179). O Fāṭir of the heavens and the earth, I ask You by Your power with which You originated the celestial and the terrestrial engendered beings, and by the right of the first Word /fol. 56r./ with which You originated the heavens and the earth

— by Your word, the Truth: Then He turned to the heaven, it being smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly (Q 41:11) — make for me that which is such-and-such. Then you mention your need: it will be fulfilled, by the leave of God, glorified and exalted. And God knows best.
